title: Book 1, Chapter 4 — From the end of the Persian to the beginning of the Peloponnesian War—The Progress from Supremacy to Empire
paragraphs: This is how Athens came to be in the position from which her power grew. The Medes had returned from Europe, beaten by the Hellenes on sea and on land, and those who had fled with their ships to Mycale had been destroyed. Leotychides, king of the Lacedaemonians, who had commanded the Hellenes at Mycale, then went home with the allies from Peloponnese. The Athenians, however, and the allies from Ionia and Hellespont, who had by now revolted from the King, stayed behind and laid siege to Sestos, which the Medes still held. They wintered before it, and when the barbarians evacuated the place they took it. After this they sailed away from Hellespont, each to their own cities. Meanwhile the Athenian people, now that the barbarian had left their country, at once began to bring back their children and wives, and whatever property they had left, from the places where they had put it for safety, and prepared to rebuild their city and their walls. For only isolated stretches of the circuit had been left standing, and most of the houses were in ruins. A few remained, and these were the ones in which the Persian grandees had taken up their quarters.

The Lacedaemonians saw what the Athenians were about to do and sent an embassy to Athens. They would themselves have preferred that neither Athens nor any other city should have a wall, but in this they acted mainly at the urging of their allies, who were alarmed by the strength of her newly acquired navy and by the valor she had shown in the war with the Medes. They asked Athens not only to refrain from building walls for herself, but also to join them in pulling down the walls that were still standing in the cities outside Peloponnese. They did not declare the real meaning of their advice, which was suspicion of the Athenians. What they urged was that in the event of a third invasion the barbarian would then have no strong place to use as his base, as he now had in Thebes, and that Peloponnese would be enough for all as a base both for retreat and for attack. The Lacedaemonians spoke in this way, and on the advice of Themistocles the Athenians immediately sent them away with the answer that they would send ambassadors to Sparta to discuss the question. Themistocles told the Athenians to send him off to Lacedaemon with all speed, but not to dispatch his colleagues as soon as they had chosen them; they were to wait until they had raised the wall to the height from which defense was possible. In the meantime the whole population of the city was to work on the wall: the Athenians, their wives and their children, sparing no building, private or public, that could be of any use to the work, but tearing everything down. He gave these instructions and added that he would answer for everything else there, and then he left. When he arrived at Lacedaemon he did not seek an audience with the authorities, but tried to gain time and made excuses. Whenever anyone in the government asked him why he did not appear in the assembly, he said that he was waiting for his colleagues, who had been held up in Athens by some business; that he expected them to arrive soon, and wondered that they were not yet there. At first the Lacedaemonians believed Themistocles, because of their friendship for him. But when others arrived, all plainly declaring that the work was going on and was already rising to some height, they did not know how to disbelieve it. Aware of this, he told them that rumors are deceptive and should not be trusted; they should send some reputable men from Sparta to inspect the work and bring back a report that could be trusted. They dispatched them accordingly. Themistocles then sent secret word to the Athenians about these men, telling them to detain them as far as possible without putting them under open constraint, and not to let them go until he and his colleagues had returned. For his colleagues had now joined him, Abronichus, son of Lysicles, and Aristides, son of Lysimachus, with the news that the wall was high enough; and he feared that when the Lacedaemonians heard the facts, they might refuse to let him go. So the Athenians detained the envoys as his message had said, and Themistocles had his audience with the Lacedaemonians. At last he told them openly that Athens was now fortified well enough to protect its inhabitants. Any embassy that the Lacedaemonians or their allies might wish to send to Athens in future should proceed on the assumption that the people they were visiting could tell both its own interests and the general interests. When the Athenians had thought it right to abandon their city and embark in their ships, he said, they had taken that dangerous step without consulting the Lacedaemonians; and on the other hand, wherever they had deliberated together with the Lacedaemonians, they had proved themselves second to none in judgment. They now thought it right that their city should have a wall, and that this would be better for the citizens of Athens and for the Hellenic confederacy alike; for without equal military strength it was impossible to contribute equal or fair counsel to the common interest. It followed, he observed, that either all the members of the confederacy should be without walls, or the present step should be accepted as right.

The Lacedaemonians showed no open anger against the Athenians at what they heard. Their embassy, it seems, had been meant not to obstruct, but to guide the counsels of the Athenian government. Besides, Spartan feeling toward Athens was at that time very friendly, because of the patriotism she had shown in the struggle with the Mede. Still, the defeat of their wishes could not fail to cause them secret annoyance. The envoys of each state went home without complaint.

So the Athenians walled their city in a short time, and the building still shows the haste with which it was done. The foundations consist of stones of every kind; in some places they are neither worked nor fitted, but set down just in the order in which the various workers brought them. Many columns from tombs and many sculptured stones were built in with the rest. The city’s bounds had been extended on every side, and so in their haste they seized on everything without exception. Themistocles also persuaded them to finish the walls of Piraeus, which had been begun earlier, in the year when he was archon. Two things influenced him: the excellence of a site with three natural harbors, and the great start the Athenians would gain in the acquisition of power by becoming a naval people. He was the first to venture to tell them to stick to the sea, and he began at once to lay the foundations of the empire. It was on his advice, too, that they built the walls as thick as they can still be seen around Piraeus; two wagons meeting each other brought up the stones. Inside the walls there was neither rubble nor mortar. They were built of great stones hewn square and fitted together, and clamped to each other on the outside with iron and lead. Only about half the height he intended was completed. He meant their size and thickness to keep off enemy attacks. A small garrison of invalids, he thought, would defend them adequately, and everyone else would be free for service in the fleet. For the fleet claimed most of his attention. He saw, as I think, that the king’s army would find the approach by sea easier than the approach by land, and he thought Piraeus more valuable than the upper city. Indeed, he was always advising the Athenians that if a day should come when land forces hard pressed them, they should go down into Piraeus and defy the world with their fleet. In this way the Athenians completed their wall, and they began their other buildings immediately after the retreat of the Mede.

Meanwhile Lacedaemon sent out Pausanias, son of Cleombrotus, as commander-in-chief of the Hellenes, with twenty ships from Peloponnese. The Athenians sailed with him with thirty ships, and so did a number of the other allies. They made an expedition against Cyprus and subdued most of the island. Afterwards they attacked Byzantium, which the Medes held, and forced it to surrender. All this took place while the Spartans were still supreme. But the violence of Pausanias had already begun to be disagreeable to the Hellenes, above all to the Ionians and the newly liberated peoples. These went to the Athenians and asked them, as their kinsmen, to become their leaders and to check any attempt at violence by Pausanias. The Athenians accepted their proposals. They resolved to put down any attempt of the kind and to settle everything else as their interests might seem to require. In the meantime the Lacedaemonians recalled Pausanias, to investigate the reports that had reached them. Hellenes arriving in Sparta had brought many grave accusations against him, and by all appearances he had acted more like a despot than like a general. His recall happened to come just when the hatred he had aroused had made the allies desert him and range themselves beside the Athenians; only the soldiers from Peloponnese stayed with him. On his arrival at Lacedaemon he was censured for his private acts of oppression, but he was acquitted on the heaviest counts and pronounced not guilty. It must be known that the charge of Medism was one of the principal articles against him, and by all appearances one of the best founded. Even so, the Lacedaemonians did not restore him to his command. They sent out Dorkis and certain others with a small force, but these found that the allies no longer wished to grant them the supremacy. They saw this and departed, and the Lacedaemonians sent no one out to succeed them. They feared that anyone who went out would deteriorate as Pausanias had. Besides, they wanted to be rid of the Median War, and they were satisfied that the Athenians were fit for the position and were at that time friendly to themselves.

Thus the Athenians had succeeded to the supremacy because the allies, hating Pausanias, gave it to them of their own will. They then fixed which cities should contribute money against the barbarian and which should contribute ships. The professed object was to retaliate for their sufferings by ravaging the King’s country. It was at this time that the Athenians first instituted the office of “Treasurers for Hellas.” These officers received the tribute, as the money contributed was called. The tribute was at first fixed at four hundred and sixty talents. The common treasury was at Delos, and the congresses were held in the temple. Their supremacy began with allies who were independent, and who acted on the resolutions of a common congress. Between the Median War and the present war, it was marked by the following undertakings in war and in administration: against the barbarian, against their own rebel allies, and against those Peloponnesian powers that came into contact with them on various occasions. I relate these events, and venture on this digression, for this reason: all my predecessors have left this part of history out, confining themselves either to Hellenic history before the Median War or to the Median War itself. Hellanicus, it is true, did touch on these events in his Athenian history, but he is rather brief and not accurate in his dates. Besides, the history of these events explains how the Athenian empire grew.

The Athenians, under the command of Cimon, son of Miltiades, began by besieging and capturing Eion on the Strymon from the Medes, and they made slaves of its inhabitants. Next they enslaved Scyros, the island in the Aegean with a Dolopian population, and colonized it themselves. A war against Carystus followed; the rest of Euboea stayed neutral, and the war ended with a surrender on conditions. After this Naxos left the confederacy. A war followed, and she was forced to return after a siege. This was the first case in which the terms of the alliance were broken by the subjugation of an allied city, and the others followed the precedent as circumstances dictated. Of all the causes of defection the chief was failure to pay tribute and supply ships, and failure to serve when called on. The Athenians were very severe and exacting, and they made themselves offensive by applying the screw of necessity to men who were not used to continuous labor, and in fact not disposed to it. In some other respects also the Athenians were no longer the popular rulers they had been at first. If they did more than their fair share of the service, it was correspondingly easy for them to reduce any who tried to leave the confederacy. The allies had themselves to blame for this. Most of them wished to get off service, and so arranged to pay their share of the expense in money in place of ships, in order to avoid leaving their homes. The result was that Athens increased her navy with the funds they contributed, while any revolt found them without resources or experience for war.

The next events were the actions by land and sea at the river Eurymedon, between the Athenians with their allies and the Medes. The Athenians won both battles on the same day under the command of Cimon, son of Miltiades, and captured and destroyed the whole Phoenician fleet of two hundred vessels. Some time afterward the Thasians defected. The cause was disagreements about the markets on the opposite coast of Thrace and about the mine that they held. The Athenians sailed to Thasos with a fleet, defeated the Thasians at sea and landed on the island. About the same time they sent ten thousand settlers, drawn from their own citizens and the allies, to settle the place then called Ennea Hodoi or Nine Ways, and now Amphipolis. They won possession of Ennea Hodoi from the Edonians. But when they advanced into the interior of Thrace, the assembled Thracians cut them off at Drabescus, a town of the Edonians; the Thracians regarded the settlement of Ennea Hodoi as an act of hostility. Meanwhile the Thasians, beaten in the field and besieged, appealed to Lacedaemon and asked her to help them by invading Attica. Lacedaemon promised, without informing Athens, and intended to do it, but the earthquake prevented her. With it came the secession to Ithome of the Helots and of the Thuriats and Aethaeans of the Perioeci. Most of the Helots were descended from the old Messenians who had been enslaved in the famous war, and so all of them came to be called Messenians. The Lacedaemonians were thus engaged in a war with the rebels in Ithome. In the third year of the siege the Thasians obtained terms from the Athenians: they razed their walls, delivered up their ships, and arranged to pay at once the money demanded and tribute in future. They also gave up their possessions on the continent together with the mine.

In the meantime the Lacedaemonians found that the war against the rebels in Ithome was likely to last. They called on their allies for help, and especially on the Athenians, who came in some force under the command of Cimon. They summoned the Athenians so urgently because of their reputed skill in siege operations. A long siege had taught the Lacedaemonians that they themselves lacked this art; otherwise they would have taken the place by assault. This expedition gave rise to the first open quarrel between the Lacedaemonians and Athenians. Assault had failed to take the place, and the Lacedaemonians became apprehensive of the enterprising and revolutionary character of the Athenians. They also regarded them as of alien extraction, and began to fear that if the Athenians stayed, the besieged in Ithome might tempt them to attempt some political changes. So they dismissed them alone of the allies. They did not declare their suspicions, but merely said that they had no further need of them. The Athenians, however, realized that their dismissal did not come from the more honorable of the two possible reasons, but from suspicions that had been formed. They went away deeply offended, conscious that they had done nothing to deserve such treatment from the Lacedaemonians. The instant they returned home they broke off the alliance that had been made against the Mede and allied themselves with Sparta’s enemy Argos; each of the contracting parties took the same oaths, and made the same alliance with the Thessalians.

Meanwhile the rebels in Ithome could no longer prolong their resistance, which had lasted ten years, and surrendered to Lacedaemon. The conditions were that they should leave Peloponnese under safe conduct and never set foot in it again; anyone found there afterward was to be the slave of his captor. It must be known that the Lacedaemonians had an old oracle from Delphi, telling them to let go the suppliant of Zeus at Ithome. So the rebels went out with their children and wives. Athens, hating the Lacedaemonians as she now did, received them and settled them at Naupactus, which she had lately taken from the Ozolian Locrians. The Athenians gained another addition to their confederacy in the Megarians. These left the Lacedaemonian alliance because they were annoyed at a war about boundaries that Corinth had forced on them. The Athenians occupied Megara and Pegae, and built the Megarians their long walls from the city to Nisaea, where they placed an Athenian garrison. This was the principal reason why the Corinthians conceived such a deadly hatred against Athens.

Meanwhile Inaros, son of Psammetichus, was a Libyan king of the Libyans on the Egyptian border, with his headquarters at Marea, the town above Pharos. He brought about a revolt of almost the whole of Egypt from King Artaxerxes, placed himself at its head, and invited the Athenians to help him. They were at that moment engaged in an expedition to Cyprus with two hundred ships of their own and their allies; they abandoned it and arrived in Egypt. They sailed from the sea into the Nile and made themselves masters of the river and of two-thirds of Memphis. Then they set about attacking the remaining third, called White Castle. Inside it were Persians and Medes who had taken refuge there, and Egyptians who had not joined the rebellion.

Meanwhile the Athenians made a landing from their fleet at Haliae, and a force of Corinthians and Epidaurians engaged them; the Corinthians won. Afterward the Athenians fought the Peloponnesian fleet off Cecruphalia, and the Athenians won. War then broke out between Aegina and Athens. A great battle was fought at sea off Aegina between the Athenians and the Aeginetans, each supported by their allies, and the Athenians won it. They took seventy of the enemy’s ships, landed in the country and began a siege under the command of Leocrates, son of Stroebus. The Peloponnesians wanted to help the Aeginetans, and threw into Aegina three hundred heavy infantry who had earlier served with the Corinthians and Epidaurians. Meanwhile the Corinthians and their allies occupied the heights of Geraneia and marched down into the Megarid. They believed that, with a large force away in Aegina and Egypt, Athens could not help the Megarians without raising the siege of Aegina. But the Athenians did not move the army from Aegina. They raised a force from the old and young men left in the city, and marched into the Megarid under the command of Myronides. The battle with the Corinthians was a draw, and the two armies parted, each believing it had won. The Athenians, however, had if anything rather the better of it, and when the Corinthians left they set up a trophy. The elders in the Corinthian city taunted them, and goaded by this the Corinthians made their preparations and, about twelve days later, came and set up their own trophy as victors. The Athenians sallied out from Megara, cut off the party that was busy erecting the trophy, and engaged and defeated the rest. As the beaten army retreated, a considerable division, hard pressed by its pursuers, mistook the road and dashed into a field on private property. A deep trench ran all round it, and there was no way out. The Athenians knew the place. They hemmed in the front with heavy infantry, placed the light troops round in a circle, and stoned all who had gone in. Corinth suffered a severe blow here. The bulk of her army continued its retreat home.

About this time the Athenians began to build the long walls down to the sea, one toward Phalerum and one toward Piraeus. Meanwhile the Phocians made an expedition against Doris, the old home of the Lacedaemonians, which contained the towns of Boeum, Kitinium, and Erineum. When they had taken one of these towns, the Lacedaemonians came to the aid of the Dorians. Nicomedes, son of Cleombrotus, led them, commanding for King Pleistoanax, son of Pausanias, who was still a minor; they brought fifteen hundred heavy infantry of their own and ten thousand of their allies. They compelled the Phocians to give the town back on conditions, and then began their retreat. If they went by sea, across the Crissaean Gulf, the Athenian fleet might stop them. The route across Geraneia seemed scarcely safe, because the Athenians held Megara and Pegae. The pass was difficult and always guarded by the Athenians, and now the Lacedaemonians had information that the Athenians meant to dispute their passage. So they resolved to stay in Boeotia and consider which line of march would be safest. They had another reason as well. A party in Athens, hoping to put an end to democracy and to the building of the Long Walls, had secretly encouraged them. Meanwhile the Athenians marched against them with their whole levy, a thousand Argives, and the respective contingents of the rest of their allies; altogether they were fourteen thousand strong. They marched because they believed the Lacedaemonians were at a loss how to effect their passage, and because they suspected an attempt to overthrow the democracy. Some cavalry from their Thessalian allies also joined the Athenians, but these went over to the Lacedaemonians during the battle.

The battle was fought at Tanagra in Boeotia. Both sides lost heavily, and victory went to the Lacedaemonians and their allies. They then entered the Megarid and cut down the fruit trees, and returned home by way of Geraneia and the isthmus. Sixty-two days after the battle the Athenians marched into Boeotia under the command of Myronides. They defeated the Boeotians in battle at Oenophyta and became masters of Boeotia and Phocis. They dismantled the walls of the Tanagraeans, took a hundred of the richest men of the Opuntian Locrians as hostages, and finished their own long walls. Next the Aeginetans surrendered to Athens on conditions: they pulled down their walls, gave up their ships, and agreed to pay tribute in future. The Athenians, under Tolmides, son of Tolmaeus, sailed round Peloponnese and burned the arsenal of Lacedaemon. They took Chalcis, a town of the Corinthians, and in a descent upon Sicyon they defeated the Sicyonians in battle.

Meanwhile the Athenians in Egypt, with their allies, were still there, and they met with every change of fortune in war. At first the Athenians were masters of Egypt. The King sent a Persian, Megabazus, to Lacedaemon with money, to bribe the Peloponnesians to invade Attica and so draw the Athenians away from Egypt. The matter made no progress and the money was being wasted. So he recalled Megabazus with what remained of it, and sent another Persian, Megabuzus, son of Zopyrus, to Egypt with a large army. Megabuzus came by land and defeated the Egyptians and their allies in a battle. He drove the Hellenes out of Memphis and finally shut them up in the island of Prosopitis, where he besieged them for a year and six months. In the end he drained the canal of its water and diverted it into another channel. This left their ships high and dry and joined most of the island to the mainland, and he marched across on foot and took it. So the enterprise of the Hellenes came to ruin after six years of war. Of all that large host a few made their way through Libya and reached Cyrene safely, but most perished. Thus Egypt returned to its subjection to the King, except for Amyrtaeus, the king in the marshes, whom they could not capture because of the size of the marsh; the marshmen are also the most warlike of the Egyptians. Inaros, the Libyan king, who alone had brought about the Egyptian revolt, was betrayed, captured, and crucified. Meanwhile a relief squadron of fifty vessels had sailed for Egypt from Athens and the rest of the confederacy. Knowing nothing of what had happened, they put in to shore at the Mendesian mouth of the Nile. The troops attacked them from the land and the Phoenician navy from the sea. Most of the ships were destroyed, and the few that remained escaped by retreat. This was the end of the great expedition of the Athenians and their allies to Egypt.

Meanwhile Orestes, son of Echecratidas, the Thessalian king, had been exiled from Thessaly, and he persuaded the Athenians to restore him. They took their allies the Boeotians and Phocians with them and marched to Pharsalus in Thessaly. They became masters of the country, but only in the immediate neighborhood of the camp, for they could go no further for fear of the Thessalian cavalry. They failed to take the city or to achieve any of the other aims of their expedition, and returned home with Orestes having accomplished nothing. Not long after this, a thousand Athenians embarked in the vessels that were at Pegae (Pegae, it must be remembered, was now theirs) and sailed along the coast to Sicyon under the command of Pericles, son of Xanthippus. They landed in Sicyon and defeated the Sicyonians who engaged them. Then they immediately took the Achaeans with them, sailed across, and marched against Oeniadae in Acarnania and besieged it. But they did not take it, and returned home.

Three years later a truce for five years was made between the Peloponnesians and Athenians. Free now from war with Hellenes, the Athenians made an expedition to Cyprus under the command of Cimon, with two hundred vessels of their own and their allies. Amyrtaeus, the king in the marshes, asked for help, and sixty of these ships were detached to Egypt; the rest laid siege to Kitium. The death of Cimon and a scarcity of provisions forced them to withdraw from it. They sailed off Salamis in Cyprus and fought the Phoenicians, Cyprians, and Cilicians by land and sea. They won on both elements and went home, together with the squadron that had returned from Egypt. After this the Lacedaemonians marched out on a sacred war. They became masters of the temple at Delphi and put it in the hands of the Delphians. As soon as they had retreated, the Athenians marched out, became masters of the temple, and placed it in the hands of the Phocians.

Some time after this, Boeotian exiles held Orchomenus, Chaeronea, and some other places in Boeotia. The Athenians marched against these hostile places with a thousand Athenian heavy infantry and the allied contingents, under the command of Tolmides, son of Tolmaeus. They took Chaeronea and made slaves of the inhabitants, and then began their return, leaving a garrison behind. On the road, the Boeotian exiles from Orchomenus attacked them at Coronea, together with some Locrians, Euboean exiles, and others who thought as they did. The Athenians were defeated in battle; some were killed and others taken captive. By a treaty providing for the recovery of the men, the Athenians evacuated all Boeotia; the exiled Boeotians returned, and with all the rest regained their independence.

Soon afterward Euboea revolted from Athens. Pericles had already crossed to the island with an army of Athenians when news was brought him that Megara had revolted, that the Peloponnesians were about to invade Attica, and that the Megarians had cut off the Athenian garrison; only a few had escaped, taking refuge in Nisaea. Before they revolted, the Megarians had let the Corinthians, Sicyonians, and Epidaurians into the town. Pericles meanwhile brought his army back from Euboea in all haste. After this the Peloponnesians marched into Attica as far as Eleusis and Thrius, ravaging the country under the leadership of King Pleistoanax, the son of Pausanias, and went home without advancing further. The Athenians then crossed again to Euboea under the command of Pericles and subdued the whole island. They settled everything but Histiaea by agreement; the Histiaeans they drove out of their homes and occupied their territory themselves.

Not long after their return from Euboea, they made a thirty years’ truce with the Lacedaemonians and their allies, and gave up the posts they held in Peloponnese — Nisaea, Pegae, Troezen, and Achaia. In the sixth year of the truce, war broke out between the Samians and Milesians over Priene. The Milesians had the worse of it and came to Athens to complain loudly against the Samians. Some private persons from Samos itself, who wanted to revolutionize the government, joined them. So the Athenians sailed to Samos with forty ships and set up a democracy. They took fifty boys and as many men from the Samians as hostages and lodged them in Lemnos; then they left a garrison in the island and returned home. But some of the Samians had not stayed in the island and had fled to the continent. They came to an agreement with the most powerful men in the city and made an alliance with Pissuthnes, son of Hystaspes, who was then satrap of Sardis. They collected a force of seven hundred mercenaries and crossed over to Samos by night. First they rose against the commons and secured most of them; next they stole their hostages from Lemnos. After that they revolted, handed over to Pissuthnes the Athenian garrison left with them, together with its commanders, and at once prepared an expedition against Miletus. The Byzantines revolted with them.

The Athenians heard the news and at once sailed against Samos with sixty ships. Sixteen of these never engaged: some went to Caria to watch for the Phoenician fleet, and others to Chios and Lesbos with orders for reinforcements. But forty-four ships under Pericles and nine colleagues gave battle off the island of Tragia to seventy Samian vessels, twenty of them transports, which were sailing from Miletus. The Athenians won. Later they were reinforced by forty ships from Athens and twenty-five Chian and Lesbian vessels. They landed, and since they were stronger on land they surrounded the city with three walls; it was also blockaded from the sea. Meanwhile word came that the Phoenician fleet was approaching to help the Samians; indeed Stesagoras and others had left the island with five ships to bring it. So Pericles took sixty ships from the blockading squadron and left in haste for Caunus and Caria. In the meantime the Samians made a sudden sally and fell on the camp, which they found unfortified. They destroyed the look-out vessels and engaged and defeated those that were launched to meet them. For fourteen days they were masters of their own seas and brought in and carried out what they pleased. But when Pericles arrived, they were shut up again. Fresh reinforcements then came — forty ships from Athens with Thucydides, Hagnon, and Phormio; twenty with Tlepolemus and Anticles; and thirty vessels from Chios and Lesbos. The Samians made a brief attempt at fighting, but could not hold out. After a siege of nine months they surrendered on conditions: they razed their walls, gave hostages, delivered up their ships, and arranged to pay the expenses of the war by installments. The Byzantines also agreed to be subject as before.
